q: Cyclohexanone and methyl vinyl ketone are heated with NaOH in ethanol (Robinson annulation). What is the final product?
h: Step 1: Michael addition gives a 1,5-diketone. Step 2: the methyl-ketone enolate attacks the ring C=O to close a six-membered ring. Step 3: heat. Where does the C=C end up?
w: The cyclohexanone enolate adds 1,4 to MVK, giving 2-(3-oxobutyl)cyclohexanone. The enolate of the side-chain CH3 then attacks the ring C=O, closing a new six-membered ring (intramolecular aldol). With heat the β-hydroxy ketone dehydrates (E1cB) so that the new C=C is conjugated with the C=O: the bicyclic enone A (C10H14O, octahydronaphthalen-2-one).
x: This is the Michael adduct, the intermediate after step 1. Under NaOH with heat it continues to the intramolecular aldol condensation.
This β-hydroxy ketone is the aldol addition intermediate; heating with base dehydrates it to the enone.
Here the C=C is β,γ to the carbonyl. E1cB dehydration forms the C=C between the α- and β-carbons, giving the more stable conjugated enone.

q: Which starting materials give the bicyclic enone shown by a Robinson annulation (NaOH, heat)?
h: Undo the aldol (break the C=C, restore the ring C=O), then undo the Michael addition. Which ring carbon bonded to the side chain, and what is on it?
w: Retro-aldol of the enone gives the 1,5-diketone: a cyclohexanone whose α-carbon carries both the CH3 (the angular methyl) and a CH2CH2C(=O)CH3 chain. Retro-Michael splits that into 2-methylcyclohexanone (its more substituted α-carbon was the nucleophile) and methyl vinyl ketone. Michael additions run under equilibrating base, so the more substituted enolate of 2-methylcyclohexanone reacts, placing the methyl at the ring fusion.
x: With pent-3-en-2-one the extra CH<sub>3</sub> ends up on the β-carbon of the acceptor, i.e., on the new ring next to the ring fusion, not on the ring-fusion carbon.
Acrolein has no methyl ketone; after the Michael step there is no CH<sub>3</sub>C=O whose enolate can close the six-membered enone ring.
The 1,3-dione would leave an extra ketone in the product (this route gives the Wieland–Miescher ketone, C<sub>11</sub>H<sub>14</sub>O<sub>2</sub>).

q: Which compound is not a Michael acceptor?
h: A Michael acceptor has its C=C conjugated with an electron-withdrawing group, so the β-carbon is electrophilic.
w: Conjugate addition requires the C=C to be conjugated with the C=O (or C≡N), which makes the β-carbon δ+. In pent-4-en-2-one a CH2 separates the C=C from the C=O (a β,γ-unsaturated ketone), so the alkene is isolated and not electrophilic.
x: Acrylonitrile's C=C is conjugated with C≡N, so its terminal CH<sub>2</sub> is an electrophilic β-carbon.
Ethyl acrylate is an α,β-unsaturated ester, a classic Michael acceptor.
Cyclopent-2-enone is an α,β-unsaturated ketone; nucleophiles add at the ring β-carbon.

q: What is the final product of this Stork enamine sequence?
h: An enamine is a neutral enolate equivalent. Which carbon of the enamine is nucleophilic, and what does aqueous acid do at the end?
w: Pyrrolidine and cyclohexanone form the enamine. Its α-carbon (nucleophilic through the N lone pair) attacks allyl bromide by SN2, giving an iminium ion. Aqueous acid hydrolyzes the iminium back to the ketone, releasing pyrrolidine: 2-allylcyclohexanone. Because the alkylated iminium is not deprotonated again under these conditions, enamine alkylation stops cleanly at one alkyl group.
x: This tertiary alcohol would come from an allyl Grignard adding to the C=O; enamines react at the α-carbon, not at the carbonyl carbon.
Stork enamine alkylation stops after one alkylation because the product is an iminium ion, not a neutral enamine.
Enamines react at carbon; there is no oxygen on the enamine to be alkylated, and hydrolysis regenerates the C=O.

q: Which structure is the product formed when cyclohexanone is heated with pyrrolidine and a catalytic amount of acid, with removal of water?
h: A secondary amine cannot form a neutral imine. After water is lost, where must the proton come from?
w: A secondary amine adds to the C=O to give a carbinolamine, which loses water to form an iminium ion. The iminium N has no H to lose, so an α-H is removed instead, giving the neutral enamine A (C=C–N).
x: This saturated amine is the product of reductive amination (with NaBH<sub>3</sub>CN); no reducing agent is present.
The carbinolamine is an intermediate; with acid and removal of water it loses H<sub>2</sub>O.
The iminium ion is also an intermediate; loss of an α-proton gives the neutral enamine that is isolated.

q: The pyrrolidine enamine of cyclohexanone is heated with methyl vinyl ketone in dioxane, and then aqueous acid is added. What is the product?
h: The enamine is a soft nucleophile. Does it add at the C=O or at the β-carbon of the enone? No hydroxide base is present for a later aldol step.
w: The enamine α-carbon adds to the β-carbon of MVK (Stork–Michael reaction). Hydrolysis of the resulting iminium/enamine with aqueous acid gives the 1,5-diketone 2-(3-oxobutyl)cyclohexanone. Closing the second ring (Robinson annulation) requires a separate base/heat step.
x: This is the Robinson annulation product; it needs base (e.g., NaOH or NaOMe) with heat to effect the intramolecular aldol condensation after the Michael step.
Enamines, like other soft, stabilized nucleophiles, add 1,4 to enones rather than 1,2 to the C=O.
This would be the product of free pyrrolidine adding to MVK. The amine is bound up as the enamine, whose nucleophilic site is carbon.

q: Diethyl malonate and cyclohex-2-en-1-one are treated with catalytic NaOEt in ethanol. What is the major product (before any hydrolysis)?
h: Is the malonate anion a hard or a soft nucleophile? Which carbon of the enone is the soft electrophilic site?
w: The malonate anion is a stabilized (soft) nucleophile, so it adds to the β-carbon of the enone (Michael addition). Protonation of the resulting enolate at the α-carbon gives diethyl 2-(3-oxocyclohexyl)malonate, with the malonate on C3 of the cyclohexanone.
x: 1,2-Addition to the C=O is reversible for stabilized anions; the 1,4-adduct, which keeps the strong C=O bond, is the thermodynamic product.
This attaches the malonate to the α-carbon (C2). In conjugate addition the nucleophile bonds to the β-carbon (C3), and the α-carbon is protonated.
A Knoevenagel-type product requires condensation with the C=O and loss of water; malonate with an enone under catalytic base undergoes Michael addition.

q: 4-Methylpent-3-en-2-one is treated with lithium dimethylcuprate, and the reaction is then quenched with aqueous NH<sub>4</sub>Cl. What is the product?
h: Gilman reagents are soft carbon nucleophiles. Which carbon of an α,β-unsaturated ketone do they attack?
w: Lithium dialkylcuprates add a carbon group to the β-carbon of α,β-unsaturated ketones (1,4-addition), even when that carbon is disubstituted. The enolate is protonated on workup to give 4,4-dimethylpentan-2-one, with a new quaternary carbon.
x: This tertiary allylic alcohol is the 1,2-addition product typical of CH<sub>3</sub>Li or CH<sub>3</sub>MgBr, not of a cuprate.
Methyl on the α-carbon with the C=C intact would require substitution of a vinyl H; cuprates add across the C=C instead.
This is the product of reducing the C=C (adding H, not CH<sub>3</sub>); the cuprate delivers a methyl group to the β-carbon.

q: Which reagent carries out the transformation shown?
h: The product is an alcohol with the C=C still in place. Was the methyl added to the carbonyl carbon or to the β-carbon?
w: The methyl group and the OH are on the former carbonyl carbon, and the ring C=C is untouched: this is 1,2-addition. Hard, highly reactive organometallics such as CH3MgBr (or CH3Li) add directly and irreversibly to the C=O of cyclohex-2-enone, giving 1-methylcyclohex-2-en-1-ol after workup.
x: Gilman reagents add 1,4; the product would be 3-methylcyclohexanone, with the C=O retained.
LDA/CH<sub>3</sub>I alkylates an α-carbon of the ketone (C6) and keeps the C=O; it does not create an alcohol.
Malonate is a soft stabilized nucleophile that gives the Michael (1,4) adduct, and it would add a CH(CO<sub>2</sub>Et)<sub>2</sub> group, not a methyl.

q: What is the major product of this one-pot sequence (ignore stereochemistry)?
h: Conjugate addition leaves an enolate. Which carbon of that enolate is nucleophilic, and is anything there to protonate it before CH<sub>3</sub>I is added?
w: The cuprate adds CH3 to C3 (1,4-addition), generating a specific lithium enolate with its C=C between C1 and C2. No proton source is present, so this enolate is trapped by CH3I at C2, the carbon between the carbonyl and the new methyl. The product is 2,3-dimethylcyclohexanone (mainly trans).
x: 3-Methylcyclohexanone forms if the enolate is protonated (aqueous workup) instead of being alkylated; here CH<sub>3</sub>I traps it.
Methylation at C6 would need the other enolate. Conjugate addition generates the enolate regiospecifically toward C2, and it does not equilibrate at low temperature with no proton source.
This tertiary allylic alcohol is the 1,2-adduct formed by CH<sub>3</sub>MgBr or CH<sub>3</sub>Li, not by a cuprate.

q: Which pair of esters, with NaOEt followed by acid workup, gives the target by a crossed Claisen condensation as the main product?
h: Disconnect the bond between the ketone C=O carbon and the α-carbon (the CH bearing CH<sub>3</sub> and CO<sub>2</sub>Et). Which piece is the acyl electrophile and which is the ester enolate?
w: The Claisen bond joins the ketone carbonyl carbon to the α-carbon between the two C=O groups. The acyl piece is PhC(=O)–, from ethyl benzoate (no α-H, so it is only an electrophile; used in excess). The enolate piece is –CH(CH3)CO2Et, from ethyl propanoate. The product still has one H on the central carbon, so the final deprotonation drives the reaction.
x: Ethyl acetate supplies a CH<sub>2</sub>, giving ethyl benzoylacetate (no CH<sub>3</sub> on the central carbon).
Here the ring is on the α-carbon side and a CH<sub>3</sub>CO group is the acyl piece; the product would be ethyl 3-oxo-2-phenylbutanoate or its isomer, not a phenyl ketone.
Ethyl formate transfers a CHO group, giving an aldehyde. The resulting product would also have no H between the carbonyls, so the Claisen would not be driven to completion.

q: A Robinson annulation combines which two reactions, in which order?
c: Michael addition, then intramolecular aldol condensation
Intramolecular aldol condensation, then Michael addition
h: The first step joins a ketone enolate to an α,β-unsaturated ketone; the second step forms the new ring and the C=C.
w: Robinson annulation is a Michael addition of an enolate to an α,β-unsaturated ketone (usually methyl vinyl ketone), giving a 1,5-diketone, followed by an intramolecular aldol condensation that closes a cyclohexenone ring.
x: The order is reversed: the 1,5-diketone needed for ring closure exists only after the Michael step.
No ester or alkoxide leaving group is involved; the new ring forms by enolate addition to a ketone (aldol), not by acyl substitution.
A Dieckmann condensation is an intramolecular Claisen of a diester; the annulation closes the ring by an aldol reaction between two ketones.

q: The pyrrolidine enamine of cyclohexanone is treated with acetyl chloride, and the product is then hydrolyzed with aqueous acid. What is the final product?
h: The enamine's nucleophilic carbon attacks the acyl chloride. What functional group results after hydrolysis of the iminium?
w: The enamine α-carbon attacks the acid chloride (nucleophilic acyl substitution, Cl− leaves), giving an acylated iminium/enamine. Hydrolysis regenerates the ring ketone, producing the β-diketone 2-acetylcyclohexanone. Stork acylation is a mild route to 1,3-dicarbonyl compounds.
x: An enol acetate would need acylation on oxygen; the enamine has no oxygen and reacts at carbon.
One equivalent of acid chloride acylates once; the product iminium is not a nucleophile, so the second α-carbon is not acylated.
This puts an extra CH<sub>2</sub> between the ring and the acetyl group; it would come from alkylation with chloroacetone, not acylation with acetyl chloride.

q: Which pair of compounds gives the 1,5-diketone shown in one C–C bond-forming step (Michael addition, then workup)?
c: Cyclohexanone pyrrolidine enamine and phenyl vinyl ketone
Cyclohex-2-en-1-one and the enolate of acetophenone
Cyclohexanone and ethyl benzoate with NaOEt
h: Number the chain from one C=O carbon (C1) to the other (C5). The Michael bond joins the donor's α-carbon to the acceptor's β-carbon. Which bond is that?
w: A 1,5-dicarbonyl is disconnected at the bond between the α-carbon of one carbonyl and the β-carbon of the other. The ring α-carbon (C2) bonds to CH2CH2COPh, so the donor is cyclohexanone (enolate or enamine) and the acceptor is CH2=CHCOPh; the donor's α-carbon adds to the acceptor's terminal β-carbon.
x: Acetophenone enolate adds to C3 of cyclohexenone, giving 3-(2-oxo-2-phenylethyl)cyclohexanone: the side chain is on C3 and has only one CH<sub>2</sub>.
A crossed aldol with benzaldehyde gives 2-benzylidenecyclohexanone (or its β-hydroxy ketone), a 1,3-relationship, not a 1,5-diketone.
A crossed Claisen with ethyl benzoate gives 2-benzoylcyclohexanone, a 1,3-diketone.
